Neonatal individuals of the Cape dune mole-rat (Bathyergus suillus) emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 30 grams [Wwb = approximately 30 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial state typical of subterranean rodents. This initial body mass is notably low compared to the substantial adult dimensions the animals will later attain, as the species displays a considerable size range driven by a prolonged growth phase. Under stable thermal conditions within the burrow system, typically around 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the young undergo a critical developmental transition known as weaning, which marks the cessation of maternal milk provisioning and the onset of independent feeding. Weaning occurs relatively early in the life cycle, recorded at approximately 21 days after birth [tx = approximately 21 days after birth], a short nursing period that may be an adaptation to the energetic constraints of life in an underground environment where food resources are patchi at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]ly distributed. Following weaning, the suckling juveniles must quickly develop the foraging skills necessary to exploit the underground geophytes and corms that constitute their primary diet.

The reproductive biology of Bathyergus suillus is characterized by a slow pace of life, with females exhibiting a low maximum reproductive rate. Detailed observations under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] indicate that a female produces, on average, a single litter of 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter], and this reproductive event occurs roughly once per year, yielding an annual frequency of 1 litter per year [F_R_i = 1 litter per year]. This output aligns with the species’ life-history strategy, which appears to prioritize the survival and quality of offspring over high fecundity. The extended gestation period required for foetal development is another indicator of this strategy. Estimated from comparative data on related bathyergid mole-rats, the duration of pregnancy is approximately 70 days [tg = approximately 70 days] when measured at the same burrow temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a prolonged interval that facilitates significant foetal growth and organogenesis before the vulnerable neonate is born.

Growth in Bathyergus suillus proceeds gradually, with individuals eventually reaching a substantial ultimate wet weight that distinguishes them among their bathyergid relatives. The maximum adult body mass recorded for this species is 780 grams [Wwi = 780 grams], a figure that demonstrates a significant expansion from the 30-gram neonatal mass (30 grams) [Wwb = 30 grams] and reflects the considerable nutritional resources required for full somatic development. Life-history theory predicts that such a large adult size, combined with a low annual reproductive output, would be associated with an extended lifespan, and available data support this hypothesis. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' deep burrow systems, which are maintained at roughly 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for the Cape dune mole-rat is 16 years [am = 16 years]. This lifespan is exceptionally long for a rodent of its size and underscores the species' position on the slow end of the life-history continuum, likely bolstered by a predator-free subterranean existence and a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate.

The onset of sexual maturation in Bathyergus suillus is delayed relative to many other rodents, a pattern consistent with its slow life history and substantial adult body mass. Captive studies conducted at a regulated temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] have established that puberty, characterized by the first signs of gonadal activity, occurs at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth]. This period of approximately one year represents the time since birth at which individuals become physiologically capable of reproduction, though first breeding in the wild may be further deferred due to social suppression or the need to establish a territory within a colony. The prolonged juvenile phase serves an important ecological function, allowing the growing animal to accumulate sufficient body reserves and structural mass before investing energy into reproduction. Compared to the rapid maturation seen in surface-dwelling rodents of similar size, the year-long delay to puberty in this solitary, burrowing species highlights the interplay between body size evolution and the energetic constraints of a low-quality, high-fiber diet.

Comparative physiological studies of African mole-rats have placed the reproductive and developmental metrics of Bathyergus suillus in a broader evolutionary context. For example, the species’ lifespan of 16 years [am = 16 years] under stable thermal conditions is notably longer than that of the smaller naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) when both are considered relative to their respective body masses, though the latter species famously exhibits even greater extremes of longevity at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. The 780-gram ultimate wet weight (780 grams) [Wwi = 780 grams] of the Cape dune mole-rat is consistent with its role as a large, solitary forager that relies on extensive burrow networks to access widely dispersed food patches. The timing of weaning at 21 days [tx = 21 days] and the 70-day gestation (70 days) [tg = 70 days], both measured at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], represent a developmental schedule that balances the rapid independence of young against the need for sufficient in utero growth. Further research is needed to clarify how variation in burrow temperature and food availability may modulate these life-history traits across the species’ geographic range in the sandy coastal plains of South Africa.
